Keywords:
Checkpoint inhibitor
Immune-related adverse event
Toxicity
Microbiome
A B S T R A C T

Background: Multiple studies have suggested that gut microbiome may influence immune checkpoint inhibitor 
(ICI) efficacy, but its association with immune-related adverse events (irAEs) is less well studied. In this pro­
spective cohort study, we assessed whether gut microbiome composition at start, or changes during ICI, are 
associated with severe irAEs.
Methods: Stool samples of cancer patients treated with anti-PD-1 ± anti-CTLA-4 were analyzed using 16S rRNA 
gene sequencing and metagenomic shotgun sequencing. Differences in alpha and beta diversity between patients 
with and without severe irAE were assessed, as well as differential relative abundance (RA) of taxa, MetaCyc 
pathways, and seven prespecified literature-based bacterial groups including pathobionts and Ruminococcaceae.
Findings: We analyzed 497 samples of 195 patients before and soon after starting ICI, at severe irAE onset and 
after starting immunosuppression. Mean RA of the pathobionts group was significantly higher in patients who 
developed a severe irAE (8.2 %) compared to those who did not (4.8 %; odds ratio 1.40; 95 %CI 1.07–1.87) at 
baseline, and also early during ICI treatment and at severe irAE onset. A significantly stronger decrease in RA of 
Ruminococcaceae after starting ICI was observed in patients who developed a severe irAE compared to those who 
did not. RAs of Ruminococcaceae, the genus Ruminococcus, and the species R. bromii and R. callidus were 
significantly lower at severe irAE onset compared to other time points.
Interpretation: Gut microbiome dysbiosis signaled by higher RA of pathobionts and decrease in RA of Rumino­
coccaceae may predispose to severe irAEs.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) can elicit long-term survival in 
patients with cancer. However, they can also cause immune-related 
adverse events (irAEs) that can be severe (grade 3 or higher) and life- 
threatening, such as pneumonitis, hepatitis, and colitis [1,2]. Approxi­
mately 15 % of patients who receive anti-programmed cell death 
(ligand) 1 (anti-PD-(L)1) monotherapy develop severe irAEs, while 
40–60 % of patients who receive anti-PD-1 plus anti-cytotoxic 
T-lymphocyte associated protein 4 (anti-CTLA-4) combination ICI

develop severe irAEs. Despite extensive efforts, the pathophysiology of 
irAEs is not yet fully understood and no discriminative predictors of 
(severe) irAEs have been found [3,4].

The gut microbiome is hypothesized to be involved in irAE patho­
genesis, but no consensus exists on which taxa are associated with irAEs. 
Two studies have demonstrated that either fecal microbiome trans­
plantation (FMT) from wild mouse microbiome-reconstituted mice [5]
to germ free C57BL/6 mice [6] or from TRUC mice to specific pathogen 
free Balb/C mice [7] predisposes these mice to anti-CTLA-4 + anti-PD-1 
colitis. Furthermore, several patients with severe ICI-induced colitis

despite resistance to several immunosuppressants [8–12]. Oral gavage 
of Facaliumbacterium prausnitzii [13], Lactobacillus reuteri [14] or a 
mixture of four Bifidobacterium species [15] in mice mitigated dextran

sodium 
(DSS)-induced 
colitis 
provoked 
by 
anti-CTLA-4 ± anti-PD-1. Conversely, administration of Bacteroides 
intestinalis was associated with increased anti-CTLA-4 +
anti-­
PD1-induced subclinical ileal damage in mice [16]. In humans, several 
studies have described higher or lower relative abundances (RAs) before 
ICI treatment of certain Bacteroides, Bifidobacterium or other taxa in 
patients who subsequently developed irAEs, but results are conflicting, 
sometimes pointing in opposite directions [13,16–36]. Similarly, 
F. prausnitzii has been observed to be less relatively abundant at baseline 
in patients who developed irAEs compared with patients who did not in 
some cohorts [13,18,22], while the inverse was observed in others [18, 
22,28,30]. This lack of consensus may be the result of the different irAE 
definitions with respect to grade and localization (colitis versus all 
irAEs), heterogeneity of anticancer therapy, small sample sizes in com­
bination with many (low abundant) bacteria, and differences in 
geographical location, sample collection procedures, DNA extraction, 
sequencing, or analysis techniques.

Distinguishing patients who are susceptible to severe irAEs based on 
their pre-treatment microbiome may aid clinical decision making. 
Furthermore, the gut microbiome could be a tentative target to prevent 
or treat irAEs if specific microbial components involved in irAEs would 
be sufficiently characterized. In this study, we assessed the correlation 
between gut microbiome composition and severe irAEs in patients with 
cancer who received ICI. We first prespecified seven bacterial groups 
based on associations with health and disease in population-wide 
studies. We then aimed to identify bacterial groups or specific individ­
ual taxa, that were predictive at baseline of subsequent severe irAE 
occurrence. Furthermore, we analyzed changes in microbiome compo­
sition during treatment, at severe irAE onset, and after the start of 
immunosuppressive treatment, to improve understanding of the role of 
the gut microbiome in irAE pathogenesis.

Patients with cancer who started first-line anti-PD-1 + anti-CTLA-4 
combination therapy or anti-PD-1 monotherapy between October 2018 
and December 2022 were included from the ongoing prospective UNI­
CIT biobank study within the University Medical Center Utrecht, the 
Netherlands [37]. Stool samples were collected before the first cycle of 
ICI (C1; baseline), at 3–4 weeks (C2) and 6–8 weeks (C3) into treatment, 
at onset of severe irAE (tox), and median 4 days after the start of each 
consecutive immunosuppressive irAE treatment (tox_IS1 to tox_IS4). 
Samples were initially analyzed using 16S rRNA sequencing. Meta­
genomic shotgun sequencing (MGS) was additionally performed on 
samples from all combination therapy treated patients, monotherapy 
treated melanoma patients with severe irAEs, and a random selection of 
monotherapy treated melanoma patients without severe irAEs. Severe 
irAEs were defined as grade 3 or higher irAEs according to the Common 
Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5.0. For pa­
tients who were alive without severe irAE at end of follow-up, a minimal 
follow-up of ten months was required to prevent misclassification of 
severe irAE occurrence. This study was not considered subject to the 
Medical Research Involving Human Subjects Act and was approved by 
the local institutional review board (sample collection per protocol 
number 18/123, sample release permission per protocols 19/704 and 
23/200). All patients provided written informed consent.
2.2. Sample collection, DNA extraction and sequencing
Patients were instructed to collect stool samples using a Sterilin

specimen container (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), 
store them at room temperature, and hand them in within 24–48 h. After 
receipt, stool samples were aliquoted and stored at −80◦C until DNA 
extraction. DNA was extracted using the QIAamp Fast DNA stool mini kit 
(Qiagen, Venlo, the Netherlands) as previously described and stored at 
−20◦C until further analysis [38–40]. The 469 bp V3-V4 hypervariable 
regions of the 16S rRNA gene were amplified according to Fadrosh et al. 
on an llumina MiSeq platform with the Miseq Reagent Kit v3 (600-cycle; 
art: MS-102–3003; Illumina, San Diego, USA) [41]. Negative (buffer) 
controls as well as mock communities with known bacterial composition 
(ZymoBIOMICS Microbial Community Standard D6300, ZymoBIOMICS 
Microbial Community DNA Standard D6305, ZymoBIOMICS Microbial 
Community Standard II (Log Distribution) D6310; Zymo Research Cor­
poration, Orange, California, USA) and negative controls (purified 
water) were included during DNA extraction, amplification, and 
sequencing steps to detect potential contamination (none detected; data 
not shown). MGS was performed by Macrogen Europe (Amsterdam, the 
Netherlands) on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform after library 
preparation using TruSeq DNA Nano (350 bp insert; Illumina) with a run 
configuration of 2x150bp. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and MGS were 
conducted in three and two batches respectively, with comparable 
sequencing results of replicates across batches, confirming reproduc­
ibility (data not shown).

16S rRNA sequencing reads were processed using QIIME2 [42]. 
Reads were demultiplexed, denoised, and clustered based on at least 
97 % similarity using DADA2 with minimum read length truncation of 
275 and 260 for forward and backward reads respectively [43]. Tax­
onomy was subsequently assigned by aligning the amplicon sequence 
variants (ASVs) to the SILVA v138.1 16S rRNA reference database [44, 
45]. Seven bacterial groups plus one rest group (‘other’) were defined 
based on previously observed associations with general health in more 
than 8000 Dutch citizens [46] and substantiated by a meta-analysis of 
more 
than 
4000 
geographically 
diverse 
stool 
samples 
[47]
(Supplementary Table 1). Taxonomic profiling of MGS reads was con­
ducted using MetaPhlAn4, with CHOCOPhlAn v3.1 201901 as reference 
database [48,49]. HUMAnN version 3.1.1 was used for MetaCyc 
pathway profiling using UniRef90 gene annotation definitions [49].

Median follow-up time with 95 % confidence interval (CI) was esti­
mated using the reverse Kaplan-Meier method. Samples with fewer than 
7000 reads were excluded from 16S rRNA beta diversity and differential 
abundance analyses. This cut-off was based on the observed ASVs in 
relation to the number of reads (data not shown). Alpha diversities based 
on 16S rRNA data were visualized at multiple rarefaction depths but 
only tested for significance at a depth of 7000 reads. Rarefaction was not 
deemed necessary for MGS data. Differences in alpha diversities by in­
verse Simpson and Shannon indexes were tested using Wilcoxon signed 
rank tests [50–53]. Differences in beta diversities were examined using 
principal components analysis (PCA) of Euclidian distances between 
centered log ratio (CLR) transformed counts [54], principal coordinates 
analysis (PCoA) of Bray-Curtis dissimilarity [55], and (except for 
pathway analysis) PCoA of weighted UniFrac distances [56], using 
Permutation Multivariate Analysis of Variance (PERMANOVA) [57,58].

We investigated differential abundances of individual taxa and of the 
bacterial groups in separate sets of analyses. Various statistical tools to 
assess differential abundance of individual taxa exist, which all have 
their strengths and weaknesses. We used four of these tools after 
excluding taxa that were prevalent in less than 10 % of the samples: 
Analysis of Compositions of Microbiomes with Bias Correction 
(ANCOM-BC) [59], Linear Model for Differential Abundance Analysis of 
High-dimensional Compositional Data (LinDA) [60], Microbiome

Multivariable Association with Linear Models 2 (MaAsLin2) using a 
linear model with total sum scaling normalization and logarithmic 
transformation [61], and ANOVA-Like Differential Expression analysis 
version 2 (ALDEx2) [62,63]. Aiming to find associations that were 
consistent across these tools, we visualized estimates of all tools for taxa 
that were differentially abundant according to Benjamini-Hochberg 
(BH) corrected p-values in at least one of them [64]. Since ANCOM-BC 
and ALDEx2 cannot accommodate longitudinal models, only LinDA 
and MaAsLin2 were used for longitudinal analyses as detailed in the 
Supplementary Methods.

Differential abundances of the bacterial groups were assessed in a 
similar manner in logistic regression and linear mixed effect models 
after CLR-transformation and imputation of zeros as described in the 
Supplementary Methods.

All differential abundance analyses were corrected for ICI type (anti- 
PD-1 + anti-CTLA-4 combination therapy or anti-PD-1 monotherapy). 
All analyses were conducted in R version 4.3.2.

In total, 497 samples from 195 patients were analyzed. Seventy-one 
patients received anti-PD-1 + anti-CTLA-4 combination therapy and 124 
received anti-PD-1 monotherapy (Figure 1). Not all patients provided 
samples at all time points. 16S rRNA sequencing yielded sufficient read 
count in 149 baseline samples and 274 follow-up samples; 49 and 84, 
respectively, were from patients who received combination therapy 
(Table 1). MGS was conducted on 89 baseline samples and 182 follow- 
up samples; 52 and 108, respectively, were from patients who 
received combination therapy (Supplementary Table 2).

The overall 16S rRNA alpha diversity of all samples combined was 
160 by Inverse Simpson and 6.2 by Shannon index. The most relatively 
abundant genera according to the 16S rRNA data were Bacteroides (mean 
RA at baseline 10 %), Faecalibacterium (8.4 %), and Blautia (7.9 %). The 
most relatively abundant species according to the MGS data were 
F. prausnitzii (mean RA at baseline 6.7 %), Bacteroides uniformis (4.3 %), 
Prevotella copri (4.2 %), Ruminococcus bromii (3.7 %), and Bacteroides 
vulgatus (3.5 %).

Alpha and beta diversities based on 16S rRNA data did not change 
after starting ICI (Figure 2a,b). A marginal but statistically significant 
decrease in the RAs of five genera were observed according to LinDA but 
not MaAsLin2, including Odoribacter (mean RA 0.20 % at baseline 
versus 0.14 % at the second cycle of ICI), Parabacteroides (1.4 % vs 
1.1 %), and Alistipes (2.0 % vs 1.9 %; Figure 2c). The RAs of the pre­
specified bacterial groups remained stable after starting ICI (Figure 2d; 
Supplementary Table 3).
3.3. Microbiome differences between combination and monotherapy

At baseline, no differences in alpha diversity, beta diversity, or RAs 
of individual taxa or bacterial groups between combination therapy and 
monotherapy were observed with 16S rRNA data or MGS data 
(Supplementary Figures 1 and 2; Supplementary Table 4). Furthermore, 
changes in gut microbiome composition after starting either combina­
tion therapy or monotherapy were not statistically significantly different 
(Supplementary Figure 3; Supplementary Table 5).
3.4. Microbiome at baseline and subsequent development of severe irAEs

The 149 patients with baseline 16S rRNA data had a median follow- 
up of 33 months (95 %CI 26–37) and 38 experienced severe irAEs during

follow-up. We observed no baseline differences in alpha diversity or beta 
diversity in patients who subsequently experienced severe irAEs 
compared to patients who did not (Figure 3a,b). The former group did, 
however, have marginal but statistically significantly higher baseline 
RAs of five genera according ANCOM-BC, but not according to the other 
tools (Figure 3c). Marvinbryantia was significantly more relatively 
abundant in patients who developed severe irAEs (mean RA 0.207 %) 
than in patients who did not (0.128 %) according to two of four tools 
(Figure 3c). Baseline RAs of neither Bacteroides nor Faecalibacterium 
were associated with subsequent occurrence of severe irAEs. No asso­
ciations at species level or of MetaCyc pathways with subsequent 
development of severe irAEs were observed using the MGS data 
(Supplementary Figure 4).

In the bacterial group analyses using 16S rRNA data, higher baseline 
mean RA of the pathobionts group was associated with subsequently 
developing severe irAEs (mean RA 8.2 % vs 4.8 %; odds ratio [OR] 1.40; 
95 %CI 1.07–1.87), but this association was no longer significant after 
correction for multiple testing (corrected p-value 0.059; Figure 4a,b; 
Supplementary Table 6). A higher baseline mean RA of the Clos­
tridiaceae group was also associated with subsequent development of 
severe irAEs (OR 1.19; 95 %CI 1.05–1.37), but the mean RAs were low 
in both groups (0.84 % vs 0.71 %) and the difference was not statisti­
cally significant after correction for multiple testing (corrected p-value 
0.059; Figure 4c). The baseline mean RA of the Ruminococcaceae group 
was similar in patient who subsequently developed severe irAEs 
(17.7 %) compared to those who did not (17.6 %; OR 0.92; 95 %CI 
0.57–1.61; corrected p-value 0.766; Figure 4d). When analyzing patients 
who received anti-PD-1 + anti-CTLA-4 combination therapy and those 
who received anti-PD-1 monotherapy separately, results were compa­
rable (data not shown).
3.5. Gut microbiome changes preceding severe irAEs

Fifty-three of the 195 patients developed a severe irAE. Patients who 
did or did not develop severe irAEs did not have different alpha or beta 
diversity trajectories over time according to both the 16S rRNA and MGS 
data (Supplementary Figures 5 and 6). However, the change in mean 
RAs of nine genera from baseline to the second ICI cycle was signifi­
cantly different in patients who developed severe irAEs compared to 
patients who did not in LinDA, but not MaAsLin2, using 16S rRNA data 
(Figure 5a). For example, the mean RA of Enterococcus increased from 
0.291 % at baseline to 0.929 % early after starting ICI in patients who 
subsequently developed a severe irAE but decreased from 0.549 % to 
0.087 % in patients who did not. Contrarily, the mean RA of Marvin­
bryantia decreased from 0.207 % to 0.168 % in patients who developed 
a severe irAE, but increased from 0.128 % to 0.160 % in patients who 
did not. No differences in mean RAs were observed at species level using 
MGS data, or when analyzing patients who received combination ther­
apy and monotherapy separately.

In the bacterial group analyses using 16S rRNA data, the mean RA of 
the Ruminococcaceae group decreased from baseline to the second ICI 
cycle in all patients, but this was more pronounced in patients who 
developed severe irAEs (from 17.7 % to 15.5 %) compared to patients 
who did not (from 17.6 % to 17.7 %; crude and corrected p-values for 
interaction 0.018 and 0.123, respectively; Figure 4d; Supplementary 
Table 7). However, the decrease in patients who developed severe irAEs 
was not statistically significant (crude and corrected p-values 0.078 and 
0.464, respectively). The mean RA of the pathobionts group did not 
change significantly from baseline to the second ICI cycle in patients 
who developed a severe irAE (from 8.2 % to 9.7 %; crude p-value 0.817) 
or in those who did not (from 4.8 % to 4.6 %; crude p-value 0.793; crude 
p-value for interaction 0.260; Figure 4b).
3.6. Microbiome changes during severe irAE episodes

therapy. Of these 17 patients, eight had colitis, three pancreatitis/dia­
betes mellitus, two meningitis and the remaining four gastritis, derma­
titis, hypophysitis, and myositis, respectively. 16S rRNA data were 
available for 15 of these 17 samples and MGS data for all 17 samples.

In individual taxa analyses comparing the 16S rRNA data of the 15 
samples that were collected at onset of a severe irAE with the 387 
samples that were collected at at baseline and all other follow-up time 
points, eight genera were differentially abundant (Figure 5b). For 
example, the mean RA of Haemophilus was significantly higher at irAE 
onset (0.31 %) compared to other time points (0.06 %), and the mean 
RA of Ruminococcus was significantly lower at irAE onset (1.26 %) 
compared to other time points (2.28 %).

Forty species were significantly more or less relatively abundant in 
the 17 samples that were collected at severe irAE onset compared to the 
228 samples that were collected at other time points in LinDA or 
MaAsLin2 models using MGS data (Supplementary Figure 7). In line 
with 16S rRNA data, two species of Ruminococcus (R. bromii and 
R. callidus) were less relatively abundant at irAE onset than at other time 
points. Contrarily, Haemophilus parainfluenzae was more relatively 
abundant at severe irAE onset (mean RA 0.25 %) than at other time 
points (0.02 %) according to both analysis tools. Interestingly,

H. parainfluenzae was detected in 13/17 (76.5 %) samples at irAE onset, 
and in only 87/228 (38 %) samples at other time points. Although the 
mean RAs of the genus Veillonella and the Veillonellaceae group did not 
differ between severe irAE onset and other time points in the 16S rRNA 
data, the mean RAs of three Veillonella species (V. parvula, V. atypica, and 
V. dispar) were significantly higher at irAE onset according to both 
LinDA and MaAsLin2. Despite being statistically significantly differen­
tially abundant, these results should be interpreted with caution given 
the low RAs of these taxa.

In the bacterial group analyses using 16S rRNA data, a lower mean 
RA of the Ruminococcaceae group was observed at onset of severe irAEs 
(13.1 %) compared to other time points (17.7 %; crude and corrected p- 
value 0.016 and 0.055, respectively; Supplementary Table 8). Similarly, 
the mean RA of the Clostridiaceae group was lower at severe irAE onset 
(0.54 %) compared to other time points (0.73 %; corrected p-value 
0.0002). The mean RA of the pathobionts group was not significantly 
higher at severe irAE onset (11.3 %) compared to other time points 
(5.3 %; crude and corrected p-value 0.104 and 0.244, respectively).

In the nine patients with samples collected at severe irAE onset and 
after immunosuppressive treatment, no common patterns in the 16S 
rRNA and MGS individual taxa analyses, or bacterial group analyses, 
could be identified, although alpha diversity was low in some patients 
after irAE onset (Supplementary Figure 8).

In this prospective cohort study of 195 patients receiving ICI, higher 
relative abundance was observed of a prespecified group considered 
pathobionts before ICI initiation in patients who developed a severe irAE 
compared to those who did not, although no longer significant after 
correction for multiple testing. Furthermore, a stronger decrease in the 
Ruminococcaceae group after ICI initiation was found in patients who 
subsequently developed a severe irAE than in those who did not. 
Additionally, we observed lower mean RAs at severe irAE onset than at 
other time points of the Ruminococcaceae group, the genus Rumino­
coccus, and two species belonging to this genus: R. bromii and R. callidus. 
Thus, a shift in gut microbiome compositions with decreased abundance 
of Ruminococcaceae may predispose to severe ICI-induced toxicity.

We hypothesized that not one single species, but an imbalance be­
tween pro-inflammatory bacteria and commensals would predispose to 
irAEs. Therefore, we were interested whether an enrichment for bacteria 
known to be immunogenic under certain circumstances could be asso­
ciated with severe irAEs. We clustered these pathobionts in one group 
based on prior observations in large population-based studies [46,47]. 
We observed a higher RA of the pathobiont group before ICI initiation in 
patients who subsequently developed severe irAEs. This numerically 
higher mean RA persisted after treatment and at onset of severe irAEs 
but could not be allocated to one specific taxa.

Interestingly, whereas reduction of Ruminococcaceae was associated 
with severe irAEs in our cohort, abundance of F. prausnitzii was not. As a 
member of Ruminococcaceae, F. prausnitzii has repeatedly been reported 
to be less abundant in patients with inflammatory bowel disease [65, 
66]. Therefore, F. prausnitzii has been hypothesized to have a protective 
role against ICI-induced toxicity and colitis in particular. Being one of 
the most abundant bacteria in the human gut, F. prausnitzii is considered 
to have anti-inflammatory properties, mainly due to the production of 
butyrate [67,68]. Gao and colleagues reported reduced abundance of 
F. prausnitzii in 10 patients with ICI-induced colitis compared to 30 
patients without, with a similar trend in an independent cohort of 34 
patients [13]. Furthermore, they observed that F. prausnitzii strain

patients with anti-CTLA-4-induced severe colitis than in 19 patients 
without, while the inverse was observed for F. prausnitzii strain L2–6. 
Furthermore, Simpson and colleagues reported lower absolute abun­
dance of F. prausnitzii in 16 Australian patients with anti-PD-1 + anti-­
CTLA-4-induced severe irAEs compared to 55 without, but the inverse 
was observed when assessing RA and for certain Ruminococcus and 
F. prausnitzii ASVs in the Dutch part of this study consisting of 32 pa­
tients. Taken together, specific strains of F. prausnitzii may predispose to 
irAEs including ICI-colitis, while others may be protective.
We found no relevant changes in gut microbiome composition before

and after starting either combination therapy or monotherapy which is 
in line with previous reports [18,20,26,30,69–71]. Although we 
observed some other statistically significant differences, their implica­
tions are yet uncertain. For example, H. parainfluenzae was more rela­
tively abundant at severe irAE onset than at other time points. As the 
mean RA of this species did not increase prior to severe irAE onset, it is 
ambiguous whether H. parainfluenzae genuinely predisposes for severe 
irAEs or is just a reflection of autoimmunity, change in stool consistency, 
or hospitalization. The mean RA of Marvinbryantia at baseline was 
significantly higher in patients who developed a severe irAE than in 
patients who did not. However, this difference was small and dissolved 
quickly after checkpoint inhibitor initiation, which may suggest a

coincidental finding. Similarly, despite a trend towards higher mean RA 
of the Clostridiaceae group at baseline in patients who developed severe 
irAE, its abundance was lower at severe irAE onset than at all other time 
points, although limited by small numbers. These statistically significant 
differences are particularly disputable, since most of them involved taxa 
with low RA. Error rates increase logarithmically with each PCR cycle 
and are therefore particularly high for low-abundant taxa. Therefore, 
caution is needed when interpreting microbiome analysis results, spe­
cifically if sample size is limited.

Despite the analysis of almost five hundred samples in 195 patients, 
numbers may be too small to dissect truly relevant patterns from coin­
cidental findings. Data from previous large population-based cohorts

enabled us to reduce the many dimensions of the microbiome to just 
seven bacterial groups, thereby increasing statistical power. However, 
this is an inherent oversimplification of the species- or even strain- 
specific pathogenicity. Other techniques that enrich for strains that are 
supposedly immunogenic, such as IgA sequencing, may help to define 
bacterial groups of interest based on a biologic rationale [72].

Taken together, in this prospective study, we observed that dysbiosis 
was associated with developing a severe irAE, signaled by a higher 
relative abundance of pathobionts before starting immune checkpoint 
inhibitors and a decreasing relative abundance of Ruminococcaceae 
during treatment.
